results.markdown:
Title: AVOD vs. SVOD vs. TVOD: What each model means for advertisers

URL Source: https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/avod-vs-svod-vs-tvod

Published Time: 2026-10-23T15:34:47+00:00

Markdown Content:
## TL;DR: What to know about AVOD, SVOD, TVOD, and FAST

*   Ad-supported streaming is growing as viewers move away from traditional TV and increasingly choose lower-cost streaming options with ads.
*   Streaming models differ in how viewers access content and how advertisers can reach them. AVOD and FAST are ad-supported, while TVOD is ad-free.
*   Advertisers can buy streaming inventory through direct IOs, programmatic guaranteed deals, PMPs, and open auctions.
*   Platforms like StackAdapt help advertisers manage AVOD and FAST inventory across publishers, making it easier to expand reach.

Nearly half of all TV advertising now happens on streaming platforms. In the first quarter of 2026, [73% of total TV viewing](https://www.nielsen.com/news-center/2026/nielsens-q1-2026-ad-supported-gauge/) in the US was ad-supported, with streaming accounting for 46.6% of that ad-supported viewing. And by 2027, [connected TV](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/integrate-connected-tv) (CTV) will represent [49.7% of TV advertising](https://chart-na1.emarketer.com/c/369303/ctv-will-account-more-than-half-of-converged-tv-ad-spending-by-2028-369303).

But it can be difficult for advertisers to understand and take advantage of the opportunities ad-supported streaming presents. With acronyms like AVOD, SVOD, TVOD, and FAST being thrown around loosely and [CTV inventory](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/connected-tv-inventory) varying widely in availability, advertisers are often unsure about what they can actually buy when it comes to streaming.

If you’re wondering what the differences are between AVOD, SVOD, TVOD, and FAST, read on to learn which models carry ad inventory and how to access it.

## What is VOD?

Video on demand (VOD) is an [over-the-top](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/ott-advertising-blog) (OTT) content delivery method that allows the viewer to choose when they watch something, as opposed to tuning into a scheduled program. That user-initiated delivery stands in contrast to linear channels like traditional cable broadcasts, which offer scheduled delivery.

OTT includes content delivered over the internet—rather than via broadcast television, cable networks, or satellites—and watched on devices like computers or smart TVs. CTV is a subset of OTT.

In 2026, streaming hit a [record high of 48.6%](https://www.nielsen.com/news-center/2026/streaming-embarks-on-annual-summer-ascent-in-nielsens-may-2026-gauge-reports/) of total TV watch-time. The rise in streaming has lowered [traditional linear TV](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/linear-tv-vs-connected-tv) consumption, which has led to new opportunities for advertisers. In fact, [EMARKETER](https://www.emarketer.com/chart/c/369303/ctv-will-account-more-than-half-of-converged-tv-ad-spending-by-2028-369303) reports that CTV ad spend is expected to surpass linear TV for the first time by 2028.

[CTV advertising](https://www.stackadapt.com/connected-tv-advertising) specifically targets viewers using a CTV device. Because CTV content is often viewed on larger screens in a more relaxed environment, CTV ads are typically known for having higher ad recall and tolerance.

But the way viewers access CTV content isn’t all the same.

There are multiple business layers within VOD, primarily subscription video on demand (SVOD), advertising-based video on demand (AVOD), and transactional video on demand (TVOD). The first letter in each abbreviation indicates how the content is funded or accessed—whether through a subscription, advertising, or individual transaction—and each model offers advertisers different opportunities and audiences to reach.

Let’s break down the details of each.

## What is SVOD?

With SVOD, viewers pay a recurring fee for unlimited access to a content library. Popular SVOD streamers include Netflix, Disney+, Amazon Prime Video, HBO Max, Paramount+, Hulu, and Peacock.

SVOD platforms are practically ubiquitous, with [90% of US households](https://www.deloitte.com/us/en/insights/industry/technology/digital-media-trends-consumption-habits-survey.html) paying for at least one SVOD service and subscribing to four services on average.

Known for their exclusive premium content, these streaming platforms traditionally generated revenue solely through subscription fees, which meant they were largely closed to advertisers. But in the last couple of years, many platforms have introduced more affordable ad-supported tiers that cost less for viewers to stream content, opening the door to advertisers.

## What is AVOD?

AVOD delivers content that is free—or available at a significantly lower cost—to consumers in exchange for watching ads. With the growth of ad-supported tiers on SVOD platforms, AVOD and SVOD are no longer separate services, but the same services sold two different ways.

Common AVOD providers include The Roku Channel, [Tubi](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/tubi-ctv-inventory-integration), and Pluto TV, as well as the aforementioned ad-supported tiers of streamers like Netflix, Disney+, and Amazon Prime Video.

Ad-supported tiers give advertisers access to highly engaged audiences and premium inventory, which typically comes with higher CPMs (but more precision than traditional TV advertising).

Inventory can be sold either through direct sales and upfronts, which may involve significant spending commitments, or programmatically through [demand-side platforms](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/demand-side-platform) like [StackAdapt](https://www.stackadapt.com/best-demand-side-platform-dsp). Programmatic options can include [fixed-price guaranteed buys](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/programmatic-guaranteed) or biddable auctions on the open internet or private marketplaces.

Due to the low cost of access, the AVOD audience is broad and wide-reaching. In fact, audiences spend more time with ad-supported TV than with ad-free TV. [Nielsen](https://www.nielsen.com/news-center/2026/nielsen-launches-2026-upfront-planning-series-with-new-datato-help-marketers-and-agencies-unlock-growth-innovation-opportunities/) recently reported that adults ages 18 to 49 spend 63.8% of their TV time with ad-supported TV, highlighting the value exchange viewers are willing to make to access the content they want to watch.

In the AVOD model, advertising revenue helps platforms fund content and operations while giving brands access to viewers through high-impact ad placements. Because advertisers cover the cost of access, they serve as the primary revenue engine. This dynamic transforms viewers from paying customers into engaged audiences—giving advertisers access to a broad pool of viewers across premium streaming environments.

For advertisers, the inventory environment combines the scale of traditional television with the targeting capabilities of digital media. AVOD platforms also maintain lighter ad loads, typically capping commercial time at [four to eight minutes per hour](http://mediapost.com/publications/article/402820/study-reveals-similar-ad-loads-for-fast-channels-v.html)—providing better brand recall and stronger return on ad spend without inducing [ad fatigue](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/ad-fatigue). When campaigns are managed through platforms like StackAdapt, which support frequency capping and brand safety controls, advertisers can also reduce repetitive exposure, keeping placements aligned with appropriate content.

## What is FAST?

Like AVOD, [FAST](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/free-ad-supported-streaming-tv-for-marketers) provides ad-supported content to viewers. But the main distinction between FAST and AVOD comes down to how content is delivered, not funding.

Both models rely on advertising revenue to provide content at reduced or no cost to viewers, but FAST delivers content continuously according to a programmed schedule with limited on-demand streaming options. In contrast, AVOD is entirely on demand, allowing viewers to select what they want to watch whenever they want.

From a media buying perspective, this delivery difference can influence how brands plan, target, and value inventory across both environments.

### What is the content mix of AVOD vs. FAST?

FAST content tends to rely heavily on a library of older content, niche thematic channels, news programming, and, increasingly, sports coverage. It continues to rapidly scale, with the number of FAST channels [growing 17.5% year-over-year (YoY)](https://www.nielsen.com/news-center/2026/fast-sports-programming-surges-at-more-than-twice-the-rate-of-sports-channel-growth/) to 2,172 channels globally in 2026.

Premium AVOD, on the other hand, provides access to an array of on-demand programming, including current-season releases,

Title: AVOD vs SVOD Explained: Streaming Ad Guide (2026)

URL Source: https://adwave.com/resources/avod-vs-svod

Published Time: 2025-12-13T00:00:00+00:00

Markdown Content:
When you boil it down, the **AVOD vs. SVOD** discussion comes down to one simple question: who pays? With **AVOD** (**Advertising-based Video on Demand**), the viewer watches for free, and advertisers foot the bill. With **SVOD** (**Subscription-based Video on Demand**), the viewer pays a regular fee for an ad-free experience.

It’s a fundamental split in business models. The path a streaming service takes determines whether its main goal is to attract the biggest possible audience for advertisers or to build a loyal, paying community around its content.

## Decoding the Dominant Streaming Models

The shift from scheduled broadcasts to on-demand libraries has completely changed how we watch TV. This new era is built on two primary business models (AVOD and SVOD) and each one creates a totally different dynamic for viewers, content creators, and the advertisers trying to reach them.

Getting a handle on these models is important for any business planning to advertise on streaming platforms. Your strategy, budget, and expectations will all be shaped by the model you’re working with.

### The Two Sides of the Streaming Coin

*   **AVOD (Advertising-based Video on Demand):** This is the "free-to-watch" model. Platforms like Tubi, Pluto TV, and YouTube offer vast libraries of content at no charge to the viewer. The entire operation is funded by selling ad inventory that runs before, during, or after a show. It's essentially the modern version of broadcast TV, just with the massive advantage of on-demand viewing.

*   **SVOD (Subscription-based Video on Demand):** Here, viewers pay a recurring fee (usually monthly or yearly) for access to a curated library of content. The big draw for subscribers is a premium, uninterrupted experience with no ads. For platforms like Netflix and Disney+, this creates a predictable revenue stream that allows for huge investments in high-production, exclusive original content.

Let's break down the key differences between these two approaches.

### At a Glance Comparing AVOD and SVOD Fundamentals

As you can see, the choice between AVOD and SVOD is a strategic one, trading broad reach for predictable revenue.

This handy infographic provides a great visual breakdown of the core differences.

The chart really highlights how AVOD casts a wide net by removing the price barrier, while SVOD is all about creating a premium, exclusive environment that people are willing to pay for.

Of course, the lines are starting to blur, with many SVOD services now offering cheaper, ad-supported tiers. But the lessons learned from traditional television are more relevant than ever, especially when it comes to making ads that people will watch. To understand the roots of this, it's helpful to learn about [what is linear TV advertising](https://adwave.com/resources/what-is-linear-tv-advertising) and see how it set the stage. Today, services like **Adwave** give local businesses the power to tap into AVOD’s massive audience, bringing sophisticated targeting to a market that was once out of reach.

> **Key Takeaway:** The AVOD vs. SVOD choice isn't just about money. It's a strategic decision between grabbing the largest possible audience with free, ad-supported content or cultivating a smaller, highly engaged group of paying subscribers.

## How AVOD and SVOD Make Money

When you look under the hood, the financial engines running AVOD and SVOD platforms couldn't be more different. Their entire approach to growth, content, and the user experience stems from how they generate cash. One model is a game of massive scale, while the other is all about cultivating deep, paying relationships.

Understanding these mechanics is the key to seeing why certain platforms behave the way they do, from the size of their content libraries to the design of their user interfaces.

### AVOD: The Economics of Scale

The AVOD business model is a numbers game, plain and simple. Revenue comes almost entirely from **advertising impressions and sponsorships**. Success isn't measured by individual subscribers, but by the sheer volume of viewers a platform can attract and the number of ads it can serve them.

To make this work, AVOD services have to achieve immense scale. By offering content for free, they tear down the biggest barrier to entry: cost. This strategy pulls in a broad, diverse audience, which in turn creates the huge inventory of ad slots needed to make real money. Each ad shown might only contribute a tiny fraction of a cent, so profitability hinges on serving billions and billions of impressions.

A huge chunk of this ad delivery is automated through sophisticated systems. Concepts like [programmatic advertising](https://virtualadagency.com.au/what-is-programmatic-advertising/) are central to how these platforms efficiently turn eyeballs into revenue.

### SVOD: The Power of Predictable Income

In sharp contrast, the SVOD model is built on **predictable, recurring revenue from subscriptions**. This steady cash flow is what allows platforms to pour massive amounts of money into high-budget, exclusive content designed to attract and (more importantly) _keep_ subscribers. For an SVOD service, it's not about total viewers; it's about paying customers.

Metrics like **Average Revenue Per User (ARPU)** and **churn rate** (the percentage of subscribers who cancel) are the lifeblood of this model. A low churn rate means the service is consistently delivering value. This creates intense pressure to constantly release compelling new shows and movies, as the platform has to justify its monthly fee to every single user, every single month.

> **Key Insight:** The core strategic tradeoff is clear. AVOD chases broad audience reach to maximize ad impressions, while SVOD focuses on deep subscriber relationships to lock in recurring, high-value revenue.

### Comparing Core Financial Metrics

To really get the AVOD vs. SVOD financial debate, it helps to put their primary metrics side-by-side.

These different financial goals show up clearly in market trends. In the global streaming services market, SVOD still commands a dominant **49% share of viewers** with over **620 million active users**. At the same time, AVOD trails at **29%** but is growing at a blistering **34% year-on-year**, especially in more price-sensitive markets. This data shows SVOD's strength in using exclusive content and family plans to keep churn low. You can find more details on [these streaming market trends here](https://www.marketgrowthreports.com/market-reports/streaming-services-market-114855).

This explosion in AVOD viewership points to a massive opportunity for advertisers. The model's real power comes from its reliance on technology to place ads effectively. This often involves sophisticated techniques to insert commercials directly into content streams. To learn more, check out our guide on [what is dynamic ad insertion](https://adwave.com/resources/what-is-dynamic-ad-insertion). This is exactly where a platform like **Adwave** comes in, giving local businesses access to this growing AVOD audience and using precision targeting to make sure ads hit the right viewers without needing a Hollywood-sized budget.

## The Advertiser's Guide to AVOD Opportunities

For any advertiser weighing their options, the AVOD vs. SVOD discussion isn't just academic, it's about budget, reach, and the very real success of a campaign. While SVOD platforms operate like exclusive clubs behind a paywall, AVOD services swing the doors wide open. This creates a massive, diverse playground for brands to play in.

This accessibility is really AVOD’s ace in the hole. It gives advertisers a golden opportunity to connect with millions of viewers who are flocking to free, on-demand streaming.

The main attraction is the sheer scale. By ditching subscription fees, these platforms pull in a huge cross-section of viewers, from dedicated cord-cutters to families just looking to add more entertainment without another monthly bill. All that reach means a massive inventory of ad slots, which gives you more shots on goal to get your message in front of the right people.

![Image 1: A man monitors an AVOD ad preview dashboard with charts and a map on a large wall-mounted screen.](https://media.adwave.com/fia320z3blxi/63AG9j1A3Jw8SFGDj86V0Z/7948b3166981a4f51dcc822e88cd33a4/avod-vs-svod-avod-analytics.jpg)
What's more, this is a whole different ballgame than old-school broadcast TV. The targeting is far more sophisticated. Instead of just buying a spot during a popular show and hoping for the best, you can pinpoint audiences based on their demographics, viewing habits, and even their specific geographic location with incredible accuracy.

results.title: AVOD vs SVOD: which is growing faster in 2026
results.markdown:
Title: AVOD vs SVOD: which is growing faster in 2026

URL Source: https://adwave.com/resources/avod-vs-svod-growth

Published Time: 2026-10-17T00:00:00+00:00

Markdown Content:
In the AVOD vs SVOD comparison, ad-supported streaming is growing faster than ad-free subscription streaming in the US. At premium SVOD services that offer an ad plan, ad plans drove 78% of net subscriber additions over the nine quarters to Q1 2026, according to [Antenna’s Adds & Ads report](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/6756b521db09e280168a4cf3/6a1dec96cc28852a8ec381e4_Antenna%20x%20State%20of%20Subscriptions%20-%20Adds%20and%20Ads.pdf).

Meanwhile, overall premium SVOD growth slowed to 7% in 2025, down from 12% in 2024, according to [Antenna’s Q1 2026 data reported by Quantumrun](https://www.quantumrun.com/consulting/streaming-industry-statistics/).

## What AVOD and SVOD mean

AVOD is advertising video on demand. Viewers pick shows and movies whenever they like, and ads pay for the content, so the service is free or cheaper than an ad-free plan. SVOD is subscription video on demand. Viewers pay a recurring fee for access to a library.

The two models now overlap. Most large subscription services sell a cheaper ad-supported tier next to an ad-free one.

A subscriber on one of those cheaper tiers pays a subscription, so subscription data counts them as SVOD. For an advertiser, though, that person watches in an ad-supported environment. Each research firm draws this line in a different place, so keep the overlap in mind when you read any AVOD vs SVOD figure. Our [AVOD and SVOD streaming ad guide](https://adwave.com/resources/avod-vs-svod) covers the models in more depth.

FAST (free ad-supported streaming TV) means free, scheduled channels with ad breaks, similar to cable. If the formats are new to you, start with [OTT advertising explained](https://adwave.com/resources/what-is-ott-advertising). For the ad units themselves, see [how in-stream video ads work](https://adwave.com/resources/in-stream-advertising).

## How we compared the sources

We make Adwave, which sells advertising across TV, search, social and the web. We have an interest in streaming ads growing, so we have kept each source’s own metric and date rather than blending them into a single number. We used recent dated public figures we could confirm. Each source measures something different:

*   Antenna measures US premium paid subscriptions by plan type. Its Q2 2026 Adds & Ads report, published in June 2026, is its latest on ad plans. Its Specialty SVOD data, covered in August 2026, has its latest figures on smaller services.
*   MoffettNathanson’s ad spending projection comes from CTAM’s roundup, which cites MediaPost.
*   Media Dynamics, listed in the same CTAM roundup, covers upfront ad dollars for streaming and linear TV.
*   eMarketer covers US CTV upfront ad spending.

We don’t merge subscriptions, revenue and spend into one growth rate. No public, dated source compares all AVOD, including FAST, with all SVOD on a single metric. Antenna’s split of paid subscriptions by plan type is the closest direct comparison.

The subscription data shows ad plans taking most of the growth while premium SVOD as a whole slows. Each row below keeps its own period and scope.

![Image 1: Couple on a sofa in a warmly lit living room choosing something to watch on TV](https://media.wavefront.adwave-apps.com/ws/ws_adwave/87f163201d41031aa61f60fa574a875fbe8434530ab87db7976d1ade5ecbf89d.jpg)

| Measure | Figure | Source and period | Scope |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| US ad-supported streaming plans | More than 110M | Antenna, Q2 2026 report | Excludes Amazon Prime Video |
| Ad plans’ share of subscriptions | 48%, up 2 points year over year and 9 points over two years | Antenna, as of March 2026 | Premium SVOD services that offer an ad plan |
| Ad plans’ share of gross additions | 59% | Antenna, Q1 2026 | Premium SVOD services that offer an ad plan |
| Ad plans’ share of net additions | 78% (50.4M of 64.8M) | Antenna, nine quarters to Q1 2026 | Premium SVOD services that offer an ad plan |
| Premium SVOD subscribers who have used an ad plan | 78% | Antenna, Q2 2026 report | At some point in the past four years |
| Specialty SVOD subscriptions | 42M, up 14% year over year | Antenna, Q2 2026 | Smaller paid services outside Netflix, Disney+, Prime Video and Hulu |
| Premium SVOD subscriber growth | 7% in 2025, down from 12% in 2024 | Antenna, Q1 2026 report | US premium SVOD |

The ad plan rows come from [Antenna’s Q2 2026 ad plans report page](https://www.antenna.live/reports/q226-state-of-subscriptions-adds-ads). The full [Adds & Ads report PDF](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/6756b521db09e280168a4cf3/6a1dec96cc28852a8ec381e4_Antenna%20x%20State%20of%20Subscriptions%20-%20Adds%20and%20Ads.pdf) supplies the 50.4M and 64.8M net-addition counts and the year-over-year changes. The Specialty SVOD figures come from Antenna data reported by [TheDesk in August 2026](https://thedesk.net/2026/08/antenna-state-of-streaming-q2-report/), and the 2025 premium growth rate from Quantumrun’s summary of Antenna’s Q1 2026 report.

Antenna counts Specialty services separately from Premium ones. These figures cover paid services only and exclude Prime Video and free apps.

Price helps explain the pull toward ads. As of September 2026, Netflix’s ad plan cost $8.99 a month against $19.99 for its Standard ad-free plan, according to [Fortune’s September 2026 streaming price roundup](https://fortune.com/2026/09/09/streaming-service-prices-2026-cord-cutting-cable/). Fortune put eight major services at $139.41 a month without ads, or $89.92 using each service’s standard ad-supported plan where one exists.

Ad-tier subscribers stay nearly as long as ad-free ones. In its Q2 2026 report, Antenna says the early worry that ad-supported subscribers would be lower quality “has not materialized,” and that they have “near identical retention rates” to ad-free subscribers.

Antenna’s Adds & Ads report puts numbers on that. After 12 months, 37% of subscribers who joined an ad plan were still subscribed, compared with 39% of those who chose ad-free. Retention is low for both plan types, which means services keep re-acquiring the same viewers, and ad tiers now take most of those sign-ups.

Cord cutters show the same lean toward ads. Among people who cancelled pay TV and didn’t move to a virtual pay TV service, Antenna found that within 90 days 43% had an ad-supported premium SVOD plan, 30% had only an ad-free plan and 27% had no premium SVOD at all. That 27% may still watch ads on free streaming apps, which Antenna’s premium SVOD data doesn’t track.

## Ad revenue and spending in streaming

Most of the money figures here are projections, not results, so read each with its date.

![Image 2: Small business owner planning an advertising budget with a notebook at a sunlit table](https://media.wavefront.adwave-apps.com/ws/ws_adwave/d7ec77ddb8767510b21b1714b6b39df6bbc5b04994f2567d92f299dd2ca4890f.jpg)

MoffettNathanson projected AVOD spending would rise 17% in 2025, to more than $15 billion across 11 streaming platforms, according to [CTAM’s ad-supported streaming roundup](https://www.ctam.com/industry-resources/media-behaviors-and-industry-trends/video-streaming-consumer-trends/the-ad-supported-streaming-market/), which cites MediaPost from October 2025.

On the buying side, eMarketer’s [Q2 2026 digital video forecast](https://www.emarketer.com/content/digital-video-forecast-trends-q2-2026) projected that US CTV upfront ad spending ($17.73 billion) would exceed primetime linear TV upfront spending ($16.98 billion) in 2026 for the first time. CTAM’s roundup also lists Media Dynamics figures of $17.2 billion in streaming upfront dollars against $16.6 billion for linear.

CTV spending covers more than AVOD, including ads on many apps and devices. These dollar figures show money moving toward streaming. They can’t be ranked against Antenna’s subscription growth rates, because they measure a different thing.

## Free streaming and FAST

Subscription data leaves out free AVOD entirely, so FAST needs its own measure. Comscore data reported in [eMarketer’s FAQ on FAST](https://www.emarketer.com/content/faq-on-fast--how-free-streaming-tv-reshaping-ad-market-2026) put US FAST viewing at 1.8 billion hours in August 2025, up 43% year over year. eMarketer names the Roku Channel, Tubi and Pluto TV among the platforms in the category, and notes that advertiser adoption has lagged behind that audience growth.

![Image 3: Suburban street at dusk with TV light glowing in several living room windows](https://media.wavefront.adwave-apps.com/ws/ws_adwave/4c3fdbc4d6ab5b1c34ddafd62bf7640c9af3036716555f935805709019a34d65.jpg)

That is a viewing-hours figure, not a count of households or subscribers, so it can’t sit in the same column as Antenna’s plan counts. It is also a national total, far wider than what a single campaign buys, so it helps to know [what reach means

Published Time: 2025-11-28T00:00:00+00:00

Markdown Content:
*   5.7%

Paid SVOD share of TV viewing

*   3.3x

Paid streaming leads over free streaming

Free ad-supported streaming services (FAST) now capture 5.7% of total TV viewing in the United States, while paid subscription streaming (SVOD) commands approximately 19% of viewing share, according to [Nielsen Gauge data](https://www.nielsen.com/news-center/2025/streaming-reaches-historic-tv-milestone-eclipses-combined-broadcast-and-cable-viewing-for-first-time/). Together, these segments represent the majority of streaming's record 47.3% total TV share. However, the growth trajectories tell a more nuanced story: free streaming is growing faster than paid, with FAST services like Tubi, Pluto TV, and The Roku Channel gaining share while traditional SVOD growth plateaus. For advertisers, this shift represents an expanding opportunity to reach premium streaming audiences without premium price barriers.

## What the data shows

The comparison between free and paid streaming reveals a market in transition, with advertising-supported models gaining momentum.

Nielsen's Gauge report tracks viewing across all streaming platforms:

**Free streaming (FAST/AVOD):**

*   Combined FAST share: 5.7% of total TV viewing (May 2025)

*   The Roku Channel: 2.8% share

*   Tubi: 2.2%+ share

*   Pluto TV: Approximately 1.0% share

*   Free tiers of paid services add additional share

**Paid streaming (SVOD):**

*   Netflix: 7.9% share (pure subscription, though now has ad tier)

*   Amazon Prime Video: 3.1% share

*   Disney+: 1.9% share

*   Hulu: 2.1% share (hybrid model)

*   Max, Peacock, Paramount+: Collectively approximately 4%

The total streaming market represents 47.3% of TV viewing, with free services capturing roughly 23% of streaming's overall share and growing.

### Growth trajectories

The two segments show different growth patterns:

**Free streaming growth:**

*   FAST platforms grew from 3.7% of TV viewing (February 2024) to 5.7% (May 2025)

*   54% growth in just 15 months

*   Tubi viewing up significantly year-over-year

*   FAST-using monthly active households up 12% YoY, according to [Wurl research](https://www.streamtvinsider.com/content/fast-using-monthly-active-households-12)

*   Nearly 50% of US households now watch FAST channels weekly

**Paid streaming growth:**

*   SVOD subscriber growth has plateaued in mature markets

*   Netflix added subscribers but growth rate slowing

*   Disney+ subscriber count stable

*   Average revenue per user flat: $65.21 (2023) to $67.66 projected (2028), according to [PwC research](https://www.pwc.com/gx/en/industries/tmt/media/outlook.html)

### Revenue comparison

Revenue tells a different story than viewership:

**Current revenue:**

*   Global SVOD: Approximately $150 billion annually

*   Global premium AVOD: Approximately $50 billion annually

**Projected 2029 revenue (Omdia):**

*   SVOD: $185 billion

*   Premium AVOD: $141 billion

*   Online video advertising total: $362 billion

The revenue gap is narrowing as advertising models scale and subscription fatigue limits SVOD growth.

### Platform-specific performance

Examining individual platforms reveals the competitive dynamics in each segment:

**Leading FAST platforms:**

_Tubi (Fox):_ The free streaming service has grown to 80+ million monthly active users globally, making it one of the largest FAST platforms. Tubi offers 50,000+ titles without requiring registration, reducing friction for viewers. Its acquisition by Fox in 2020 brought content advantages and integration with Fox's broader advertising sales operation.

_Pluto TV (Paramount):_ With 200+ live channels and thousands of on-demand titles, Pluto TV pioneered the linear-style FAST experience. Paramount's ownership connects Pluto to deep content libraries including CBS, Comedy Central, and MTV programming. The platform reaches over 80 million monthly active users globally.

_The Roku Channel:_ Operating on Roku's dominant connected TV platform gives The Roku Channel distribution advantages. It has grown to 2.8% of total TV viewing, benefiting from integration into the Roku home screen and remote buttons. Original content investments have increased viewer engagement.

**Major SVOD platforms:**

_Netflix:_ Despite adding an ad tier, Netflix remains primarily subscription-driven. Its 282+ million global subscribers generate the majority of revenue through monthly fees. However, the ad tier's 70+ million monthly active users represent meaningful advertising inventory growth.

_Amazon Prime Video:_ Amazon's 2024 decision to add advertising to all Prime Video viewers transformed the platform overnight into a massive ad-supported service. With 200+ million Prime members having video access, this represents the largest single ad inventory expansion in streaming history.

_Disney+ and Hulu:_ Disney's streaming strategy spans both services, with Hulu offering hybrid ad/subscription models for years and Disney+ adding an ad tier in 2022. Combined, Disney's streaming properties reach over 170 million subscribers globally.

## Breaking down the numbers

Understanding what drives each segment's performance helps advertisers make informed decisions.

### Why free streaming is growing faster

Several factors drive FAST's rapid growth:

**Subscription fatigue:** The average US household subscribes to 3-4 streaming services. Deloitte research indicates "SVOD stacking has reached its limit and will start declining in 2025." Consumers are dropping services and turning to free alternatives for content variety.

**Content quality improvement:** FAST services have invested heavily in content. Tubi now offers 50,000+ titles. The Roku Channel has expanded original programming. Pluto TV carries live channels from major networks. The quality gap between free and paid has narrowed substantially.

**Economic pressure:** Inflation and economic uncertainty make free options more attractive. When budgets tighten, entertainment subscriptions often get cut. Free streaming provides similar entertainment value without monthly fees.

**Discovery and convenience:** Smart TV integration has made FAST discovery effortless. Many viewers find FAST channels while browsing, and the friction-free access (no account required for many services) drives adoption.

### Why paid streaming growth is slowing

SVOD faces several headwinds:

**Market saturation:** In the US, streaming penetration has reached 96% of households, according to [Kantar research](https://www.kantar.com/inspiration/technology/us-video-streaming-market-contraction-in-q2-2025). Growth must come from share shifts rather than new adopters.

**Price increases:** Every major SVOD has raised prices multiple times since 2022. Netflix's standard plan now exceeds $15/month. Disney+ increased prices 27% in 2023. These increases push price-sensitive consumers toward free alternatives or ad-supported tiers.

**Content fragmentation:** Consumers must subscribe to multiple services to access desired content. This fragmentation creates frustration and drives cord-cutting from streaming services themselves.

**Ad tier cannibalization:** The most successful SVOD growth is in ad-supported tiers, not premium subscriptions. Netflix reports 70+ million monthly active users on its ad tier. This growth dilutes pure subscription revenue.

### The hybrid middle ground

Many services now straddle both categories:

*   **Netflix**: Subscription-first with growing ad tier

*   **Hulu**: Long-standing hybrid model

*   **Peacock**: Free tier available alongside premium

*   **Amazon Prime Video**: Added ads to all users in 2024

*   **Disney+**: Ad tier growing faster than ad-free

This hybridization blurs the line between free and paid, with advertising becoming central to nearly all streaming business models.

### Content availability comparison

Content libraries differ significantly between free and paid:

**Free streaming content:**

*   Older catalog titles and library content

*   Some original programming (Tubi Originals, Roku Originals)

*   Licensed content from major studios

*   Live linear channels with curated programming

*   News and sports highlights (limited live sports)

**Paid streaming content:**

*   New release films and series

*   Exclusive original programming

*   Live sports (increasingly)

*   Day-after broadcast TV (Hulu)

*   Premium film releases

The content gap has narrowed as FAST services invest in originals and secure better licensing deals. However, first-run premium content remains primarily on paid services, creating differentiation that justifies subscription fees for engaged viewers.

Title: CTV Dictionary: Your Guide to Connected TV Terms

URL Source: https://adsmanager.paramount.com/insights/what-is-ctv-advertising-definitions

Published Time: 2026-02-17T19:22:02.326Z

Markdown Content:
If you’ve ever searched “what is CTV?” or “what is CTV advertising?” you’re not alone. These terms get thousands of searches every month. (Yes, we did our SEO research. Consider this blog our official answer to the internet.)

As connected TV continues to reshape television advertising, the terminology can feel overwhelming. Between OTT platforms, CTV measurement, ROAS calculations, geo targeting, programmatic media buying, and full funnel marketing, it’s easy to get lost in the acronyms.

This CTV dictionary is your go-to reference guide. Whether you're new to streaming TV ads or refining your CTV advertising strategy, this glossary breaks down the most important terms in clear, practical language.

CTV (Connected TV) refers to any television that connects to the internet and streams video content. This includes:

*   Smart TVs
*   Streaming devices like Roku, Fire TV, or Apple TV
*   Gaming consoles
*   TVs connected to OTT platforms

In short, if a TV is streaming content through the internet, it qualifies as connected TV.

FYI: [CTV viewership](https://adsmanager.paramount.com/insights/report-ctv-advertising-vs-social-ad-performance) now represents a major share of total TV time, making it one of the most important advertising trends in modern media planning.

## CTV Ads

CTV ads are non-skippable video advertisements served within streaming TV content. They typically run for 15 or 30 seconds and appear full-screen.

[Best practices](https://adsmanager.paramount.com/insights/ctv-video-ad-creative-best-practices-holiday-advertising) to make TV ads engaging for streaming viewers:

*   Strong opening hook in the first 3–5 seconds
*   Clear, simple messaging
*   On-screen branding
*   Verbal and visual call-to-action

## CTV Ads Manager

A CTV ad manager is a campaign management advertising platform that allows advertisers to create, launch, and monitor ads across platforms. Typically includes build-in audience targeting and performance reports. Need an example? [Why not try out Paramount Ads Manager >](https://adsmanager.paramount.com/sign-up)

CTV ad measurement refers to tracking and analyzing the performance of streaming campaigns. Common CTV marketing metrics include:

### Brand Lift:

Measures the impact of advertising on awareness, perception, and purchase intent, often used to measure upper funnel impact beyond direct conversions.

### CTV CPMs (Cost per thousand impressions):

The cost to deliver 1,000 impressions with an ad.

Formula: (Total Spend ÷ Impressions) × 1,000

### CPL (Cost per lead):

The cost to generate one qualified lead from an ad.

### Impressions:

The total number of times an ad is served & seen by a viewer.

### ROAS (Return on Ad Spend):

Measures marketing investment ROI (return on investment) based on revenue generated for every dollar spent on advertising.

ROAS calculation formula: Revenue ÷ Ad Spend

### TV Attribution Analysis:

Measurement that connects CTV exposure to downstream actions such as website visits, app download, in-store visits, or purchases.

### VCR (Video Completion Rate):

The percentage of viewers who watch a video ad from start to finish.

Formula: Completed Views ÷ Total Impressions

## CTV Advertising

CTV advertising refers to video ads that run on connected TV devices through streaming services. Unlike traditional television advertising, CTV ads allow for:

*   Household-level targeting (ZIP code, age, gender, income)
*   Real-time campaign measurement and reporting
*   Attribution tracking
*   Retargeting across devices
*   Self-serve campaign creation through online advertising platforms

## CTV Audience Targeting

The ability to deliver ads based on geographic and demographic filters such as ZIP code, age, gender, or income. With CTV ad platforms like Paramount Ads Manager, you can target based on the following:

### Geo-targeting:

A targeting method that delivers ads based on geographic location, including Country, State, DMA (Designated Market Area), ZIP code, or radius targeting around a specific address. This is particularly valuable for local TV advertising and regional businesses.

### Contextual targeting:

[Contextual targeting](https://adsmanager.paramount.com/insights/ctv-contextual-targeting) serves ads based on the content being watched rather than individual user data. For example, running auto ads during sports content.

### Custom Audiences:

Custom audiences allow advertisers to target viewers using their own first-party data, like CRM email lists, website visitors, App users, and customer databases. These audiences can often be uploaded securely into a CTV advertising platform for retargeting.

### Insights & Behaviors targeting:

Uses aggregated data signals to reach viewers based on likely purchase intent or lifestyle characteristics. This targeting helps align ads with high-intent segments.

### Lookalike Audiences:

Groups of viewers who share similar characteristics with your existing customers or custom audiences. Using first-party data (like CRM lists or website visitors), advertising platforms analyze shared behaviors, demographics, or interests and identify new viewers who “look like” your best customers.

### Retargeting:

[Retargeting campaigns](https://adsmanager.paramount.com/insights/ctv-retargeting) deliver ads to users who have previously interacted with your brand. In CTV, retargeting can:

*   Re-engage website visitors on the big screen
*   Follow up CTV exposure with digital ads
*   Reinforce messaging across devices

## CTV Inventory

Connected TV inventory refers to the available ad placements within streaming TV content.

## Demand Generation

Marketing efforts designed to create awareness and interest in your product or service before a consumer is actively shopping, focusing on:

*   Brand awareness campaigns
*   Educational content
*   Thought leadership
*   Video advertising

Demand generation fuels the top of the funnel and strengthens long-term performance marketing results.

## Device Graph

Device graphs are a foundational component of modern CTV measurement and retargeting strategies, as they connect multiple devices (whether that's a connected TV, mobile phone, laptop, or tablet) to a single household or user profile.

By linking devices together, advertisers can:

*   Retarget viewers across screens
*   Measure cross-device performance
*   Improve attribution accuracy

The process of allocating budget across channels including CTV, search, and social.

## First-Party Data vs Third Party Data

### First-party data

Information a business collects directly from its own customers. Examples include:

*   Email subscribers
*   Website visitors
*   App users
*   Purchase history

First-party data is highly valuable in CTV advertising because it allows advertisers to build custom audiences and retarget known customers in a privacy-compliant way.

### Third-party data

Audience information collected and aggregated by external data providers. It is often used for:

*   Interest targeting
*   Behavioral targeting
*   In-market audience segments

As privacy regulations evolve, many advertisers are shifting toward greater reliance on first-party data in combination with contextual targeting.

## Frequency Capping

Frequency capping limits how often a viewer sees the same ad within a given time frame. (For example: No more than 3 impressions per household per day). Frequency capping helps:

*   Reduce ad fatigue
*   Improve viewer experience
*   Optimize media efficiency

## Funnel Marketing / Marketing Funnel

The practice of aligning campaigns to specific funnel stages in the customer journey:

### TOF (Top of Funnel) / Upper Funnel:

Focuses on awareness, with the goal to introduce your brand to new audiences

### MOF (Mid Funnel):

Focuses on consideration, with the goal to build trust, educate, and nurture interest

### BOF (Bottom of Funnel) / Lower Funnel:

Focuses on conversion, with the goal to drive direct action such as purchases or sign-ups

## Full Funnel Marketing

Running coordinated campaigns across all stages of the customer journey, from awareness through conversion.

## Incremental Reach

Incremental reach refers to the new audience exposure gained by adding a channel to your media mix.

In CTV advertising, incremental reach measures how many viewers you reached on streaming TV who were not exposed to your ads on social, search, or other platforms. CTV is often used specifically to:

*   Reach cord-cutters
*   Extend beyond social platform audiences
*   Reduce reliance on a single channel

## Incrementality Testing

Incrementality testing measures the true impact of an advertising channel by comparing exposed vs. non-exposed audiences.

##Media Buying Media buying is the process of purchasing advertising

results.markdown:
Title: Free ad-supported streaming: What FAST means for marketers

URL Source: https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/free-ad-supported-streaming-tv-for-marketers

Published Time: 2024-10-18T12:00:00+00:00

Markdown Content:
Streaming services have long been seen as a more cost-effective alternative to traditional cable TV packages. But after years of economic uncertainty and rising living costs, paying for programming is no longer making the cut, and viewers are looking for ways to reduce what they’re paying to consume content. If that means watching a few ads, well, bring it on.

According to [the New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2024/05/26/business/media/ads-tv-streaming.html), there were 93 million ad-supported subscriptions in the US at the end of 2023, and 56% of new streaming service subscribers chose a lower-priced ad tier in the first quarter of 2024 (an increase of 39% from a year earlier).

To date, nearly every major streaming service has introduced an ad-supported tier, decreasing the flow of subscription cancellations while increasing revenue.

But there’s a whole subset of consumers who are tired of paying for multiple streaming services (or don’t want to pay at all), and for that, they’re turning to free ad-supported streaming television (FAST).

## What is FAST?

Free ad-supported TV is a streaming service category that provides viewers with access to linear television and video-on-demand programming. Unlike traditional streaming services, viewers don’t have to sign up and pay for a subscription. Users can stream content for free. The only catch is that they have to watch more ads, similar to over-the-air and cable TV.

Once a niche, FAST streaming services now represent [4.1% of the entire TV viewership market](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/connected-tv-stats) (that’s more than Amazon Prime Video), with [one-third of the US population](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/connected-tv-stats) expected to use a FAST service at least once per month in 2024.

With such a big audience and so much inventory, marketers are beginning to realize FAST’s full potential and how it can be used as part of a [multi-channel](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/downloads/guide-to-multi-channel-advertising) or [connected TV (CTV) marketing strategy](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/connected-tv-marketing-strategies) to achieve more scale while remaining efficient with their ad spend.

### How FAST works

FAST streaming services provide viewers with access to a variety of linear TV and on-demand content—including TV shows, movies, news, and live sports—[directly through their smart TVs](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/integrate-connected-tv) or [over-the-top](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/differences-ott-ctv) devices.

Viewers can access streaming services by either downloading an app or accessing it directly from their home screen (many FAST services, like the Roku Channel or Samsung TV Plus, come pre-loaded in select smart TVs and CTV devices).

Some FAST streaming services and channels are dedicated to a specific show or category, airing reruns and curated content on a linear schedule 24 hours a day. Viewers can select what they want to watch from a channel guide, and ads are shown at set times, often before or after programming and during traditional commercial breaks, similar to cable or satellite TV.

Other streaming services offer an on-demand or hybrid viewing experience, allowing viewers to select from a library of titles in addition to streaming linear programming. Ads are dynamically inserted into the content, with advertisers targeting users based on their demographics, viewing behaviours, and geolocations.

### Differences from other streaming models

FAST’s content and commercial breaks resemble [other streaming models](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/avod-vs-svod-vs-tvod) and traditional TV, but here’s a quick overview of their key similarities and differences:

*   **Linear TV** is a traditional television format delivered via cable, over-the-air or satellite, where viewers watch scheduled programs on specific channels at designated times. It typically includes commercial breaks shown before, during, or after broadcasts.
*   **SVOD** (subscription video on demand) services like Netflix and Disney+ require a monthly or annual subscription fee to view their content. They provide access to content on-demand and don’t show ads to viewers who subscribe to ad-free plans.
*   **AVOD** (ad-supported video on demand) is a subset of SVOD that lets viewers watch content at a lower cost by showing them a certain number of ads during streaming. Most major streamers now provide lower-priced, ad-supported tiers (with the exception of Apple TV+).
*   **FAST** is a subset of AVOD. It offers linear and on-demand programming and is completely ad-supported. Viewers don’t pay, but watch more ads in exchange.

## Popular FAST platforms

Major media conglomerates, technology companies, and TV device makers are all getting in on FAST.

According to [Nielsen](https://www.nielsen.com/data-center/the-gauge/), some of the most popular FAST platforms include Tubi, the Roku Channel, and Pluto TV. Other examples of popular FAST platforms include Samsung TV Plus, Xumo Play, Vudu, Plex, LG Channels, Vizio WatchFree+, Freevee, and BBC iPlayer.

## Benefits and features of streaming with FAST

Despite a plethora of premium options, FAST continues to be a hit with streamers. Here are four of the reasons why:

### Accessibility and affordability

Because revenue is generated entirely through advertising, FAST platforms don’t require monthly subscriptions to use their services. Users don’t have to log in, and many FAST services come pre-installed on smart TVs and devices, making it more accessible for many viewers.

### Easy transition from linear TV and SVOD

FAST platforms provide user experiences and programming that are familiar to anyone who’s watched traditional linear TV or used a subscription-based streaming service before. Live and scheduled programming can be accessed from channel guides similar to traditional cable and satellite services or select TV shows and movies to watch on-demand. FAST platforms can also be accessed from various devices, including smart TVs, smartphones, and tablets. All you need is an internet connection.

### Quality programming

Unlike paid-for subscription services, which provide access to lots of original content, FAST platforms are often unfairly mischaracterized as being a dumping ground for classic TV shows and movies. Although much of the content on FAST streaming services is licensed content, research shows that the average person prefers to watch acquired content (between August 26 and September 1, 2024, [the most streamed TV show in the US](https://www.nielsen.com/data-center/top-ten/#television) was _Prison Break_, a show whose original run ended in 2009). Plus, because FAST platforms don’t rely on dual revenue streams, they’re forced to update their programming more often to appeal to more viewers and incentivize them to watch for longer periods of time.

### Broad reach

[According to Goldman Sachs and other media analysts](https://www.nbcnews.com/business/consumer/free-ad-supported-tv-pluto-tubi-freevee-xumo-rcna160729), because “cord never” members of millennial and Gen-Z cohorts (i.e., people who have never signed up for cable before) and older generations both stream content through FAST services, advertisers can gain access to a broader audience than traditional cable or paid-for streaming services alone.

## FAST trends: Reasons behind its adoption and growth

In 2018, only about [10%](https://content-na1.emarketer.com/faq-on-free-ad-supported-streaming-tv-fast) of the US population regularly streamed content through a FAST service.

Fast-forward seven years, and nearly [115.6 million Americans](https://content-na1.emarketer.com/faq-on-free-ad-supported-streaming-tv-fast) are expected to use a FAST service at least once per month in 2025. By 2028, that number will increase by 12.47%, with 35.8% of Americans projected to stream content through a FAST platform.

#### US free ad-supported streaming TV (FAST) viewers, 2022-2028

*   FAST viewers

*   % of population

Source: [EMARKETER](https://content-na1.emarketer.com/faq-on-free-ad-supported-streaming-tv-fast)

According to [EMARKETER](https://content-na1.emarketer.com/faq-on-free-ad-supported-streaming-tv-fast), part of the reason why FAST viewership has grown so much is because smart TV makers continue embedding FASTs into their operating systems, making it easy for viewers to access FAST services the second they turn on their TV.

The cost of streaming services is another factor. Recent research found that [63% of viewers](https://www.marketingtechnews.net/news/7-in-10-ctv-users-prefer-streaming-free-ad-supported-tv/) were likely to sign up for a streaming subscription service
